definition: Deft means quick and skillful in one's movements, especially with the hands.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word deft. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know deft should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The florist's deft wiring saved the drooping peonies an hour before the gallery opening.
Handy fixes the hinge and hangs the shelf — useful skill with no special finesse claimed — but deft goes further: quick, precise motions with nothing wasted.
Surgical goes further than deft — deft hands work clean and quick; surgical precision could part a knot one thread at a time.

Sure-handed praises reliability under pressure — the hands do not slip when the stakes rise. Deft asks for more than a good grip: quick, economical, precise motion. A sure-handed mover gets the mirror down the stairs intact; deft fingers retie the bow before anyone sees it slipped.

Nimble-fingered praises pure finger speed — fast, light movement and nothing else. Deft keeps the quickness but adds tidy economy: each motion is placed and none is wasted. A nimble-fingered shuffler is merely fast; a deft one makes every flick land exactly where it was aimed.

At the oyster bar, Kofi shucks to order: a deft slide of the knife at the hinge, a quarter-turn, and the shell opens unbroken with the oyster untouched in its liquor — two hundred a night, and the count of cut thumbs, he says, stands at zero since the nineties.
Deft is the exact word because deft means skillful and capable, especially with the hands — small, precise motions that land right the first time.
Quick alone could be sloppy; strong is beside the point.
Deft is economy: no wasted move, no bruised oyster, no blood.
Deft lives closest to the fingers — knots, sutures, pastry, solder.
Of its unit-mates, adroit adds cleverness and stretches to social moves, agile is the whole body at speed, adept is mastery of an entire pursuit.
If you could film the praise in close-up on two hands, the word is deft.

The first thing students notice about Mr.
Tanaka's origami demonstrations is what they don't see: hesitation.
A square of paper becomes a crane in forty folds, and his hands seem barely to move.
Each crease is placed once, pressed once, and never adjusted.
Watching a video of his deft folding at quarter speed, you realize the pace never actually drops -- the motions are simply so small and so exact that nothing looks hurried.
His students' cranes take twice as long and three times the creases.
The difference, he tells them, is not faster fingers but fewer, better moves.
